md: A metal is **atoms** held in place, with **free electrons** drifting between them: that drift is the current. The electrons keep **colliding with the atoms**. Each collision gets in the way of the flow, which is **resistance**, and hands the atom energy, which **heats** the wire.

stem: A toaster element is a metal wire carrying a current. Follow one free electron through it and explain where the resistance and the heat come from. [2]

steps.working: The free electron drifts between the metal atoms, carrying the current.
steps.decision: The current is the drift of free electrons past atoms held in place.

steps.working: It collides with a metal atom, which gets in its way: resistance.
steps.decision: Every collision holds back the flow of charge.

steps.working: The atom takes some of the electron's energy and vibrates more: the wire heats up.
steps.decision: More vibration of the atoms is what a hotter wire is.

steps.working: An electron that met no atoms would meet no resistance and heat nothing.
steps.decision: The near-miss: without collisions there would be neither effect, so both come from the same event.

prompt: When a free electron in a current-carrying wire collides with a metal atom, what two things does the collision cause?
options: resistance to the current and heating of the wire
a current that is used up and a wire that cools
extra free electrons and a lower resistance
answer: resistance to the current and heating of the wire
explain: As in steps 2 and 3 of the See it: the atom gets in the electron's way, which is resistance, and takes energy from it, vibrating more, which is heating. Nothing is used up and no electrons are made. So one collision causes resistance and heating.

optionNotes.option: a current that is used up and a wire that cools
optionNotes.why: It can feel as if the current is spent in the wire. The same charge flows on; what the atoms gain is energy, so the wire warms, never cools.

optionNotes.option: extra free electrons and a lower resistance
optionNotes.why: A collision makes no new electrons. It gets in the flow's way, so it is where resistance comes from, not a way to lower it.

twin.prompt: A free electron in the element of an electric fire collides with a metal atom. What happens to the atom?
options: it takes energy and vibrates more
it loses an electron and becomes charged
it is knocked out of the wire
twin.answer: it takes energy and vibrates more
twin.explain: The atom stays in place but takes energy from the electron, so it vibrates more. That extra vibration is the element heating up.

optionNotes.option: it loses an electron and becomes charged
optionNotes.why: The atoms in a metal stay as they are; the collision only passes them energy.

optionNotes.option: it is knocked out of the wire
optionNotes.why: The atoms are held in place in the metal. They vibrate harder about that place; they do not leave.

md: In each collision the electron passes energy to the atom, and the atom **vibrates more**: a hotter wire. So the energy a current produces in a wire is **heat** (thermal energy). A full answer names four things: **heat**, **electrons**, **atoms** and **collide**.

title: Where the marks went
md: **Summer 2025 Foundation:** many did not give heat as the energy. **Summer 2023:** most named the electrons, but many named a particle from inside the atom for the other, and only the more able said they collide.

stem: The plates of a hair straightener get hot when a current flows through the wire inside them. Name the energy produced, and describe how the particles in the wire produce it. [4]

steps.working: The energy produced is heat (thermal energy).
steps.decision: Name what the energy becomes. Electrical is what goes in, so it earns nothing here.

steps.working: Free electrons move through the wire, carrying the current.
steps.decision: The first particle: the electrons.

steps.working: They collide with the atoms of the metal.
steps.decision: What they do, and the second particle: whole atoms, never protons or a nucleus.

steps.working: Each atom takes energy and vibrates more, so the wire heats the plates.
steps.decision: The link back to heat: more vibration is a hotter wire.

prompt: A question asks why the wire in an electric blanket gets warm when a current flows. Which answer names all four things the marks are for?
options: heat is produced because the free electrons collide with the metal atoms
electrical energy is produced as the electrons move through the wire
heat is produced because the electrons collide with the protons
the current is used up in the element and turns into heat
answer: heat is produced because the free electrons collide with the metal atoms
explain: Check each answer against steps 1 to 3 of the See it: heat, the electrons, the atoms, and that they collide. Electrical energy is what goes in, protons sit inside the nucleus, and the current is never used up. Only heat from free electrons colliding with the metal atoms has all four.

optionNotes.option: electrical energy is produced as the electrons move through the wire
optionNotes.why: Electrical energy is what the wire takes in, so it feels like the answer. The mark is for what it becomes: heat. And no atoms or collisions are named.

optionNotes.option: heat is produced because the electrons collide with the protons
optionNotes.why: Protons are inside the atom's nucleus. The electrons collide with whole metal atoms, so this loses the atom mark.

optionNotes.option: the current is used up in the element and turns into heat
optionNotes.why: The current is never used up: the same charge flows on round the circuit. What the wire gains is energy from collisions.

twin.prompt: A question asks why the element of an oven grill glows red hot. Which answer names all four things the marks are for?
options: heat is produced as free electrons collide with the metal atoms
light is produced because the element has a high resistance
heat is produced as electrons collide with neutrons
heat is made because electricity is used up in the grill
twin.answer: heat is produced as free electrons collide with the metal atoms
twin.explain: The four marks are heat, electrons, atoms and collide. Only the answer with free electrons colliding with the metal atoms, producing heat, names them all.

optionNotes.option: light is produced because the element has a high resistance
optionNotes.why: The glow tempts you to say light, but the main energy is heat, and resistance names no particles or collisions.

optionNotes.option: heat is produced as electrons collide with neutrons
optionNotes.why: Neutrons are inside the nucleus. The electrons collide with whole metal atoms.

optionNotes.option: heat is made because electricity is used up in the grill
optionNotes.why: Nothing is used up: the charge flows on. The heat comes from collisions, which this does not mention.

text: 2. Twice the length, twice the resistance

md: Twice the length means twice as many atoms in the way, so twice the collisions and **twice the resistance**. For the same wire at a constant temperature, resistance is **directly proportional** to length. To find another length's resistance, go through one metre.

title: Why the graph starts at zero
md: No length means no wire, so no atoms to collide with and no resistance. That is why a graph of resistance against length for one wire is a **straight line through the origin**.

md: Tape the wire along a metre rule. The **ammeter** goes **in series**, so the current in the wire flows through it. The **voltmeter** goes **across** the length being tested, from the fixed clip to the sliding clip. For each length, read the voltmeter and the ammeter and work out $R = V \div I$.

stem: Complete the circuit for the practical: add an ammeter and a voltmeter, so that the resistance of the length being tested can be found. [2]

steps.working: Ammeter: in the main loop, in series with the wire.
steps.decision: The current has to flow through an ammeter for it to measure it.

steps.working: Voltmeter: one lead to the fixed clip, one to the sliding clip, in parallel with the tested length.
steps.decision: A voltmeter measures the push across something, so it joins either side of just that stretch of wire.

steps.working: Both readings, taken at one length, give that length's resistance.
steps.decision: Resistance is the voltage divided by the current.

prompt: In the resistance and length circuit, how is the voltmeter connected?
options: across the length of wire being tested
in series with the wire
across the cells only
answer: across the length of wire being tested
explain: As in step 2 of the See it, the voltmeter's two leads go to the fixed clip and the sliding clip, so it sits across the stretch being tested, in parallel with it. The ammeter is the one in series. So the voltmeter is across the length of wire being tested.

optionNotes.option: in series with the wire
optionNotes.why: That is the ammeter's place. A voltmeter measures the push across a component, so it joins across it, in parallel.

optionNotes.option: across the cells only
optionNotes.why: Across the cells it reads the supply, not the tested stretch, so V ÷ I would not give that length's resistance.

twin.prompt: In the same resistance and length circuit, how is the ammeter connected?
options: in series with the wire
across the length of wire being tested
across the cells only
twin.explain: The wire's current has to flow through the ammeter, so it goes in the main loop, in series. The voltmeter is the one across the tested length.

optionNotes.option: across the length of wire being tested
optionNotes.why: That is the voltmeter's place. An ammeter measures what flows through it, so it sits in the loop.

optionNotes.option: across the cells only
optionNotes.why: Joined across the cells, it would be in parallel with them. The ammeter must be in series, so the wire's current passes through it.

md: Name the variables in a fixed order: the one you **change** (independent), the one you **measure** (dependent), then the ones you **keep the same** (controls). In this practical: changed, the length; measured, the resistance; kept the same, the thickness, the material and the temperature. The length comes first, so it cannot turn up as a control.

title: Why the controls are kept the same
md: A thicker wire or a different metal has a different resistance, and a current heats the wire, which raises it. So each is kept the same, with a small current switched off between readings, and only the length changes the resistance.

stem: A heating coil in a beaker of water is switched on for 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 minutes, with the same current each time, and the rise in temperature is measured. Name the independent variable, the dependent variable and one control variable. [3]

steps.working: Independent: the time the coil is switched on.
steps.decision: It is the one set on purpose, a different value each run.

steps.working: Dependent: the rise in temperature.
steps.decision: It is read after each run.

steps.working: Control: the current (or the volume of water).
steps.decision: Kept the same, so only the time changes the rise.

prompt: A practical keeps one 1.00 m length of nichrome wire, changes the current through it and measures the voltage across it. What is the independent variable?
options: the current in the wire
the voltage across the wire
the length of the wire
explain: Use the order of steps 1 to 3 of the See it: what is changed on purpose is independent, here the current; the voltage is then read, so it is dependent; the length stays at 1.00 m, so here it is a control. The answer is the current in the wire.

optionNotes.option: the voltage across the wire
optionNotes.why: The voltage does change, but only because the current is changed: it is what is read, the dependent variable. Summer 2023's commonest wrong answer.

optionNotes.option: the length of the wire
optionNotes.why: In the length practical the length is changed; here it stays at 1.00 m, so here it is a control.

twin.prompt: A student times how long a kettle takes to boil different volumes of water, 0.5 litres to 1.5 litres. What is the independent variable?
options: the volume of water
the time taken to boil
the power of the kettle
twin.explain: The independent variable is the one set on purpose: the volume of water. The time is read, so it is dependent; the kettle's power is kept the same.

optionNotes.option: the time taken to boil
optionNotes.why: The time is what is measured each run, so it is the dependent variable.

optionNotes.option: the power of the kettle
optionNotes.why: The same kettle is used every time, so its power is kept the same: a control.

answer: doubling the current doubles the voltage
explain: Look at steps 1 and 2 of the See it: line A doubled when the length doubled, and line B did not. Proportional is that test: double one quantity and the other doubles. So doubling the current doubles the voltage.

optionNotes.option: the voltage goes up as the current goes up
